notes:
I've written notes for every verse. The coverage is uneven, though, because I ran out of searches and page fetches before I could reach several of the sites you listed. Here's what's missing:

- **Pages I never read:** netbible.org, bibleodyssey.org, newadvent.org, catholic.com, oca.org, wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed.com, the Lutheran sites (lcms.org, 1517.org), the Pentecostal sites other than enduringword.com, and preceptaustin.org. I also only saw search excerpts, not the full pages, for Gill, Ellicott, Pulpit, Poole and Keil & Delitzsch.
- **Catholic and Orthodox readings:** I only have these second-hand, as Protestant writers report them.
- **Prosperity, word-of-faith and hyper-grace teaching:** I found nothing on these for this chapter.
- **Pentecostal view:** the only source from that list is enduringword.com (David Guzik).
- **Which tradition each writer belongs to:** the pages don't say. Those labels are my own, marked "[my label]", and you should check them.

---

**Overview**
- Barnes calls the chapter a parable that parallels Jesus' parables of the great feast (Matthew 22; Luke 14). He says this closing warning ends the long introduction, and the reader is left to choose between Wisdom and Folly. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/proverbs/9.htm
- Guzik summarises the chapter as two women, Wisdom and Folly, each inviting the simple and foolish. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-9/
- *Modern scholarship:* A Themelios article on TGC says the chapter is built as a mirror: verses 13–18 reflect verses 1–6. For many years Hebrew scholars considered verses 7–12 a later addition, but the article argues they are essential to the chapter. It also cites a scholar who puts the "fear of Yahweh" at the centre of the chiasm, that is, at the centre of the mirror pattern. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/themelios/article/the-delight-of-wisdom/

**v. 1**
- *Traditional reading:* Guzik says the main point is that Wisdom's house is large, well furnished and unshakable. He adds that commentators have long been tempted to give the "seven pillars" a symbolic meaning. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-9/
- Barnes takes seven to mean completeness and perfection. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/proverbs/9.htm
- GotQuestions thinks the house most likely means a home in proper order, with "seven" stressing that it is complete and lacks nothing.  https://www.gotquestions.org/seven-pillars-wisdom.html
- *Where Protestant writers differ:* the split is between reading v. 1 as a picture of Christ and his church, and reading it plainly.
  - Reformed/Presbyterian [my label]: Poole, as quoted on Bible Hub, says the house is the church, which Christ, the Wisdom of the Father, hath erected. For him the pillars are prophets, apostles and ministers.  The Geneva Study Bible says the same: Christ has prepared a church, and the pillars are its patriarchs, prophets, apostles and pastors.  Matthew Henry calls the church Wisdom's house and thinks Solomon probably had his own temple in mind.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/9-1.htm and https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_009.cfm
  - Baptist [my label]: Gill says Christ, the Wisdom of God, is meant.  He calls the pillars ministers of the gospel and connects them to Jachin and Boaz, the two pillars of Solomon's temple.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/9-1.htm
  - Methodist [my label]: Benson takes seven as a round number for "many" pillars, showing beauty and stability.  He notes that many Church Fathers and modern writers saw the house as the church.  Adam Clarke, another Methodist commentator, as Guzik quotes him, rejects the allegories of the Fathers and medieval writers. Clarke says they produced "strange creatures of their own brain." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-9/
  - Pulpit Commentary: "spiritual writers" see here Christ's incarnation and the church as his body.  It also links the pillars to the sevenfold gifts of the Holy Spirit (Isaiah 11:2).  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/proverbs/9-1.htm
- *Catholic and medieval readings, as Protestants report them:* Keil & Delitzsch reject the old reading of the pillars as the seven sacraments. They do accept the old link to the seven gifts of the Spirit.  Clarke, as quoted by Guzik, lists the patristic and medieval readings: the house is Christ's humanity, and the pillars are the sacraments or the gifts of the Spirit. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-9/
- *Other views:* Hitzig, an older critical scholar, took the pillars architecturally, as supports around an inner court.  GotQuestions notes some see a banquet pavilion.  Others note some ancient writings described the world as resting on seven pillars, and some think the pillars are seven sections of Proverbs 1–8.  https://www.gotquestions.org/seven-pillars-wisdom.html

**v. 2**
- Barnes says the wine was mixed with myrrh and other spices for flavour and strength. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/proverbs/9.htm
- Guzik quotes Poole: the wine was mixed with spices, or with water, which may hint that Wisdom teaches self-control. Clarke adds that ancient peoples rarely drank wine unmixed with water. Guzik also quotes Waltke: slaughtering was normally a man's job, but Wisdom is an extraordinary woman. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-9/

**v. 3**
- Barnes says Wisdom and Folly (v. 13) speak from the same places to the same people: the undecided, standing where the paths to life and death divide. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/proverbs/9.htm
- Guzik quotes Trapp, who saw the maidens as ministers who preach the gospel. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-9/
- Coffman contrasts Wisdom's call from the city's high places with Folly's secretive work.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/proverbs/9-1.html

**v. 4**
- Matthew Henry says every one of us must admit we are among the "simple" who are invited.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/proverbs/9-1.html
- Bible Hub's study notes define "simple" as inexperienced but teachable.  https://biblehub.com/proverbs/9.htm
- Clarke, as Guzik quotes him, says "lacks judgment" literally means lacking a heart: someone feeble, fickle and easily drawn away. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-9/

**v. 5**
- *Traditional reading:* Barnes sees a parallel to the Gospels' higher teaching (John 6:27; Matthew 26:26). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/proverbs/9.htm
- Bible Hub's notes link it to Christ's words "I am the bread of life" (John 6:35).  https://biblehub.com/proverbs/9.htm
- Guzik grants that older commentators saw the Lord's Supper here, but calls that over-allegorising Hebrew poetry. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-9/
- *Protestant–Catholic difference:* Guzik quotes Trapp, a Puritan [my label], who uses this verse to criticise the Catholic Church for withholding the communion cup from lay people. Clarke, as quoted there, says the Fathers' reading took the bread and wine as the Lord's Supper. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-9/

**v. 6**
- Guzik says Wisdom makes the invitation, but the simple must respond. He quotes Waltke, who links it to Jesus' kingdom banquet in Luke 14. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-9/
- Kingcomments (on Bible Hub) calls it an invitation with no conditions that must be accepted without conditions. Any excuse for not coming is "folly" to be left behind.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/king-en/proverbs/9.htm

**v. 7**
- Barnes says these verses seem to interrupt the invitation, but the logic is that Wisdom speaks to the open-minded and turns away from the scorner (compare Matthew 13). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/proverbs/9.htm
- Guzik quotes Ross: the scoffer won't live by moral teaching and mocks others who do. He also quotes Kidner, who says "abuse" is a better word than "shame." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-9/

**v. 8**
- Guzik quotes Bridges: this is the rule of Christian prudence. Don't rebuke when it will do more harm than good; wait for the right moment. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-9/
- Matthew Henry says even wise people need correcting, and the wiser someone is, the more they should want their faults pointed out.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_009.cfm

**v. 9**
- Guzik compares Matthew 13:12: whoever has will be given more. He quotes Clarke: the wise are like bees that draw honey from every flower. He also quotes Trapp, who notes that David valued Nathan for his plain speaking. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-9/
- Bible Hub's notes give Apollos, who accepted correction from Priscilla and Aquila (Acts 18), as an example.  https://biblehub.com/proverbs/9.htm

**v. 10**
- Guzik says this repeats Proverbs 1:7: wisdom begins with a right relationship with God. He defines the fear as real fear, but in the sense of awe and reverence rather than cowering. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-9/
- *Readings of "the Holy One":* in Hebrew the word is plural. Trapp, quoted by Guzik, says the plural points to the Trinity. Kidner, also quoted there, says it expresses excellence, like *Elohim*, a plural Hebrew word for God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-9/ Barnes thinks the plural probably agrees with an understood *Elohim*. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/proverbs/9.htm

**v. 11**
- Matthew Henry says wisdom helps bodily health, while folly and excess shorten life.  https://www.studylight.org/commentary/proverbs/9-1.html
- Guzik says beginning with the fear of the Lord "will always be rewarded." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-9/

**v. 12**
- Barnes calls this "the great law of personal retribution." He notes that the Septuagint (the ancient Greek translation) adds extra lines to this verse. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/proverbs/9.htm
- Guzik quotes Kidner, who calls this perhaps the Bible's strongest statement of individualism. Kidner says it doesn't deny that people affect each other; it stresses that each person gains or loses most. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-9/
- Matthew Henry says the one who scorns Wisdom's offer bears the blame.  https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Pro/Pro_009.cfm

**v. 13**
- Barnes sees the harlot as a picture of the sensual life. In his view "simple" here is meant in the worst sense, and her ignorance is wilful. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/proverbs/9.htm
- Kingcomments identifies her with the "strange woman" of Proverbs 2, 5 and 7.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/king-en/proverbs/9.htm

**v. 14**
- Barnes says Folly's house is no stately palace and she has no maidens. She sits at the door herself, imitating Wisdom's voice. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/proverbs/9.htm
- Guzik quotes Waltke: chairs were rare, so her seat suggests a claim to honour. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-9/
- A homily on Bible Hub calls Folly parasitic: she makes nothing of her own and invites people to misuse what God has given.  https://biblehub.com/sermons/proverbs/9-1.htm

**v. 15**
- Guzik quotes Poole: she targets innocent people going about their business, because the corrupt come to her anyway. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-9/

**v. 16**
- Guzik says Folly copies Wisdom's call (v. 4) word for word. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-9/
- Bible Hub's notes say both women call the same people, so no one can stay neutral.  https://biblehub.com/proverbs/9.htm
- Kingcomments sees the devil here as a master imitator.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/king-en/proverbs/9.htm

**v. 17**
- Barnes calls this the besetting sin of every age: pleasures attract because they are forbidden (Romans 7:7). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/proverbs/9.htm
- Guzik quotes Kidner, who calls it the motto of the sophisticated, set against v. 10 as the motto of the wise. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-9/
- Kingcomments calls it a "prison meal" of bread and water.  https://biblehub.com/commentaries/king-en/proverbs/9.htm

**v. 18**
- Guzik admits sin has real pleasures "for a season" (Hebrews 11:25), but says they end in death. He quotes Waltke: like Satan in Genesis 3, Folly denies that sin leads to death. He also quotes Wiersbe: the guests come to a funeral, not a feast, and it is their own. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/proverbs-9/
- Bible Hub's notes connect her guests with "the spirits in prison" (1 Peter 3:19).  https://biblehub.com/proverbs/9.htm
